title: The first spy-satellite photos were caught in mid-air by a plane

cover.alt: Grainy black-and-white film still: a twin-boomed cargo plane flies through a pale sky with long poles trailing beneath it.

body: **Discoverer 14** was really a CORONA spy satellite, built to photograph the Soviet Union from orbit. It launched on 18 August 1960, and the next day, over Alaska, it dropped a capsule holding its exposed film. The capsule came down by parachute southwest of Hawaii, where a C-119 cargo plane called Pelican 9 snatched it out of the air. It was the first film recovered from an orbiting satellite, and the first object caught in mid-air on its way back from orbit.

slides.alt: Black-and-white newsreel: a cargo plane flies with long poles trailing below; the view looks down past the poles at clouds; the plane tows something on a line; a cable drum turns; a battered capsule dangles in the air.
slides.caption: From a newsreel on the first catch, August 1960: a C-119 cargo plane trails long hooks, then tows a snagged capsule as a winch reels it in.

steps.label: 17th pass, over Alaska: film capsule out
A C-119 catches it in mid-air

slides.prompt: The capsule held only 20 lb (9.1 kg) of film, half a full load. How much did it show?
slides.answer: More than every U-2 flight before it
slides.detail: It gave broader coverage of the Soviet Union than all the U-2 spy-plane missions flown until then.

slides.question: Pilot Harold Mitchell flew Pelican 9 past the falling capsule more than once. On which pass did he catch it?
slides.explanation: The third, on 19 August 1960. The parachute had been sighted about 360 miles (580 km) southwest of Honolulu.

slides.heading: A name that hid a spy
slides.text: Discoverer 14, also known as Corona 9009, was a KH-1 satellite in the Corona spy programme, run by the Pentagon’s Advanced Research Projects Agency and the US Air Force.
